source_text: Ἀνάγκη δὲ ἀπολογούμενον ἀκριβεστέρους παρέχειν τοὺς λογισμοὺς καὶ περὶ τῶν ὀνομάτων, ὅτι νεώτερα, καὶ περὶ τῶν εἰκόνων, ὅτι χθὲς καὶ πρώην γεγόνασιν, ὡς λόγῳ εἰπεῖν· ἴστε δὲ καὶ ὑμεῖς ταῦτα ἀξιολογώτερον, ὡς ἂν ἐν πᾶσι καὶ ὑπὲρ πάντας τοῖς παλαιοῖς συγγινόμενοι. Φημὶ οὖν Ὀρφέα καὶ Ὅμηρον καὶ Ἡσίοδον εἶναι τοὺς καὶ γένη καὶ ὀνόματα δόντας τοῖς ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν λεγομένοις θεοῖς. Μαρτυρεῖ δὲ καὶ Ἡρόδοτος· Ἡσίοδον γὰρ καὶ Ὅμηρον ἡλικίην τετρακοσίοις ἔτεσι δοκέω πρεσβυτέρους ἐμοῦ γενέσθαι, καὶ οὐ πλείοσι· οὗτοι δέ εἰσιν οἱ ποιήσαντες θεογονίην Ἕλλησι, καὶ τοῖσι θεοῖσι τὰς ἐπωνυμίας δόντες καὶ τιμάς τε καὶ τέχνας διελόντες, καὶ εἴδεα αὐτῶν σημήναντες. Αἱ δ᾿ εἰκόνες, μέχρι μήπω πλαστικὴ καὶ γραφικὴ καὶ ἀνδριαντοποιητικὴ ἦσαν, οὐδὲ ἐνομίζοντο, Σαυρίου δὲ τοῦ Σαμίου καὶ Κράτωνος τοῦ Σικυωνίου καὶ Κλεάνθους τοῦ Κορινθίου καὶ κόρης Κορινθίας ἐπιγενομένων· καὶ σκιαγραφίας μὲν εὑρεθείσης ὑπὸ Σαυρίου, ἵππον ἐν ἡλίῳ περιγράψαντος, γραφικῆς δὲ ὑπὸ Κράτωνος, ἐν πίνακι λελευκωμένῳ σκιὰς ἀνδρὸς καὶ γυναικὸς ἐναλείψαντος· ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς κόρης ἡ κοροπλαθικὴ εὑρέθη· ἐρωτικῶς γάρ τινος ἔχουσα περιέγραψεν αὐτοῦ κοιμωμένου ἐν τοίχῳ τὴν σκιάν, εἶθ᾿ ὁ πατήρ, ἡσθεὶς ἀπαραλλάκτῳ οὔσῃ τῇ ὁμοιότητι, (κέραμον δὲ εἰργάζετο) ἀναγλύψας τὴν περιγραφὴν πηλῷ προσανεπλήρωσεν· ὁ τύπος ἔτι καὶ νῦν ἐν Κορίνθῳ σώζεται. Τούτοις δὲ ἐπιγενόμενοι Δαίδαλος καὶ Θεόδωρος ὁ Μιλήσιος ἀνδριαντοποιητικὴν καὶ πλαστικὴν προσεξεῦρον. Ὁ μὲν δὴ χρόνος ὀλίγος τοσοῦτος ταῖς εἰκόσι καὶ τῇ περὶ τὰ εἴδωλα πραγματείᾳ, ὡς ἔχειν εἰπεῖν τὸν ἑκάστου τεχνίτην θεοῦ. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἐν Ἐφέσῳ τῆς Ἀρτέμιδος καὶ τὸ τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς (μᾶλλον δὲ Ἀθηλᾶς· Ἀθηλᾶ γὰρ ὡς οἱ μυστικώτερον, οὕτω γὰρ τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐλαίας τὸ παλαιὸν) καὶ τὴν καθημένην Ἔνδοιος εἰργάσατο μαθητὴς Δαιδάλου, ὁ δὲ Πύθιος ἔργον Θεοδώρου καὶ Τηλεκλέους, καὶ ὁ Δήλιος καὶ ἡ Ἄρτεμις Τεκταίου καὶ Ἀγγελίωνος τέχνη, ἡ δὲ ἐν Σάμῳ Ἥρα καὶ ἐν Ἄργει Σμίλιδος χεῖρες, καὶ Φειδίου τὰ λοιπὰ εἴδωλα, ἡ Ἀφροδίτη ἐν Κνίδῳ ἑταίρα Πραξιτέλους τέχνη, ὁ ἐν Ἐπιδαύρῳ Ἀσκληπιὸς ἔργον Φειδίου. Συνελόντα φάναι, οὐδὲν αὐτῶν διαπέφευγεν τὸ μὴ ὑπ᾿ ἀνθρώπου γεγονέναι. Εἰ τοίνυν θεοί, τί οὐκ ἦσαν ἐξ ἀρχῆς; Τί δαί εἰσι νεώτεροι τῶν πεποιηκότων; Τί δαὶ ἔδει αὐτοῖς πρὸς τὸ γενέσθαι ἀνθρώπων καὶ τέχνης; Γῆ ταῦτα καὶ λίθοι καὶ ὕλη καὶ περίεργος τέχνη.
pass_a_gloss: It is necessary for one making a defense to provide more precise thoughts also about the names, that they are recent, and about the images, that they came into being yesterday and the day before, so to speak; but you also know these things are more worthy of consideration, as being in agreement with all the ancients and beyond all the ancients. I say then that Orpheus and Homer and Hesiod are the ones who gave both the families and the names to the gods spoken of under them. And Herodotus bears witness: for I think Hesiod and Homer are older than me by four hundred years, and not much more; these are the ones who made the theogony for the Greeks, and gave the epithets to the gods and divided the honors and arts, and indicated the forms of them. But the images, until the plastic and graphic and statue-making arts were not yet, were not even thought of, until Saurius the Samian and Craton the Sicyonian and Cleanthus the Corinthian and a Corinthian maiden came along; and the art of shading was discovered by Saurius, who drew a horse in the sun, and the graphic art by Craton, who smeared the shadows of a man and a woman on a whitened board; and from the maiden the art of coroplasty was discovered; for having an erotic passion for someone, she drew his shadow while he was sleeping on a wall, and then her father, delighted by the exact likeness, (he worked with clay) carved out the drawing and filled it in with clay; and the model is still preserved in Corinth today. And following these, Daedalus and Theodorus the Milesian further developed the statue-making and plastic arts. But the time is so short for the images and the business of idols, as to have the craftsman of each god say so. For the one in Ephesus of Artemis and the one of Athena (or rather Athela, for Athela is the more mystical name, as the ancient one from the olive) and the seated Endoios made by a student of Daedalus, and the Pythian is the work of Theodorus and Telecleus, and the Delian and the Artemis are the art of Tectaeus and Angelion, and the one in Samos, Hera, and in Argos, the hands of Smilis, and the rest of the images are the work of Phidias, and the Aphrodite in Cnidus is the work of Praxiteles, and the one in Epidaurus, Asclepius, is the work of Phidias. To sum it up, none of these has escaped being made by a human. If then they are gods, why did they not exist from the beginning? Why are they younger than their makers? Why did they need humans and art to come into being? Earth, stones, wood, and elaborate art are what they are made of.
pass_b_english: A defender must offer a more precise account not only of the names — because they are recent — but also of the images, since they came into being, so to speak, only yesterday and the day before. You yourselves recognize these facts as even more weighty, since they harmonize with all the ancients and surpass them. I assert, then, that Orpheus, Homer, and Hesiod are the very ones who gave both the genealogies and the names to the gods spoken of under them. Herodotus bears witness: he reckons Hesiod and Homer to be four hundred years older than himself, and not much more; these are the poets who composed the theogony for the Greeks, who assigned the gods their epithets, distributed their honors and functions, and described their forms. As for images, they were not even conceived until the arts of modeling, drawing, and statue-making appeared — until Saurius of Samos, Craton of Sicyon, Cleanthus of Corinth, and a Corinthian maiden arrived on the scene. Saurius discovered shadow-drawing by tracing a horse in the sunlight; Craton invented graphic art by smearing the silhouettes of a man and a woman onto a whitened panel; the maiden originated coroplasty when, seized with erotic longing for a youth, she outlined his shadow on a wall as he slept, and her father, a potter, delighted by the exact likeness, carved the outline and filled it with clay — a model still preserved in Corinth today. Building on these, Daedalus and Theodorus of Miletus further developed statue-making and modeling. The time allotted to images and the whole idol-making enterprise is so brief that one can practically name the craftsman of each god. The Artemis of Ephesus and the Athena (or rather Athela, the more mystical name, derived from the ancient olive) — the seated statue was Endoios' work, a pupil of Daedalus; the Pythian Apollo is the work of Theodorus and Telecleus; the Delian Apollo and Artemis are the art of Tectaeus and Angelion; the Hera in Samos and the statue in Argos are the hands of Smilis; the remaining images are Phidias' work; the Aphrodite of Cnidus is the work of Praxiteles; the Asclepius at Epidaurus is the work of Phidias. In short, not one of them has escaped being made by human hands. If they are gods, why did they not exist from the beginning? Why are they younger than their makers? Why did they need human beings and art to come into being? They are earth, stone, wood, and elaborate craftsmanship — nothing more.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the parenthetical remark regarding the father's work and the specific distinction between Athena and Athela. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source.

The Greek text is correctly identified as Athenagoras' 'Plea for the Christians 17'. The translation accurately reflects the content of the source paragraph. All key elements, including names, images, and historical references, are preserved. The scripture citations are not applicable here as no biblical text is quoted. The title 'Origin of Idols' appropriately captures the content of the passage.
